sub: How the Turkish War of Independence began

slides.title: From World War I to Turkish War of Independence
slides.cap: Historical connection: Defeat and partition of the Ottoman Empire
slides.body: World War I ended with the Ottoman Empire defeated and Allied powers planning its partition. Turkish nationalists rejected that settlement and fought to establish a sovereign state in Anatolia.

stats.lbl: Defeat and partition of the Ottoman Empire
World War I ended with the Ottoman Empire defeated and Allied powers planning its partition. Turkish nationalists rejected that settlement and fought to establish a sovereign state in Anatolia.

slides.title: Before the Turkish War of Independence
slides.body:
The Ottoman defeat in World War I brought Allied occupation and plans to partition Anatolia, provoking a nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal.

The Conflict Takes Shape: The war determined whether Anatolia would be partitioned and whether a sovereign Turkish national state would replace the Ottoman order. The opening phase established the political goals, alliances, and military problems that shaped every later campaign.

title: Franco-Turkish War
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Franco-Turkish War
slides.body:
The Franco–Turkish War, known as the Cilicia Campaign in France and as the Southern Front of the Turkish War of Independence in Turkey, was a series of conflicts fought between France and the Turkish National Forces from December 1918 to October 1921 in the aftermath of World War I. French interest in the region stemmed from the Sykes-Picot Agreement and was further fueled by a refugee crisis following the Armenian genocide.

Why This Moment Matters: Franco-Turkish War was more than an isolated engagement. It helped define the conflict's direction and exposed the strengths and weaknesses of the opposing sides. The war determined whether Anatolia would be partitioned and whether a sovereign Turkish national state would replace the Ottoman order.

Consequences: The effects of Franco-Turkish War extended beyond its immediate result. Conventional war, forced migration, communal violence, and population exchange transformed Anatolia and neighboring regions. Its place in the wider campaign also influenced later military choices and political calculations.

title: Greco-Turkish War
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Greco-Turkish War
slides.body:
The Greco-Turkish War of 1919–1922 was fought between Greece and the Turkish National Movement during the partitioning of the Ottoman Empire in the aftermath of World War I, between 15 May 1919 and 14 October 1922. This conflict was a part of the Turkish War of Independence.

title: Battle of Karboğazı

slides.title: Battle of Karboğazı
slides.body:
The Karboğazı ambush, also known as Battle of Karboğazı was an engagement recorded in Turkish historiography, fought between the Turkish nationalists and the French battalion on Toros Mountains during the Turkish War of Independence. Karboğazı literally means "Snow Pass".

title: Turkish–Armenian War
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Turkish–Armenian War
slides.body: The Turkish invasion of Armenia, also known as the Turkish–Armenian War and known in Turkey as the Eastern Front of the Turkish War of Independence, was a conflict fought between the recently established First Republic of Armenia and the Turkish National Movement, following the signing of the Treaty of Sèvres in 1920. The treaty transferred vast portions of eastern Anatolia from the Ottoman Empire to Armenia, including the towns of Trabzon, Erzurum and Van. While delegates of the Ottoman government reluctantly signed the treaty following their defeat in World War I, members of the Ottoman parliament refused to ratify it. The treaty greatly angered the Turkish Nationalists, led by Mustafa Kemal Pasha, who refused to recognize it. In September 1920, remnants of the Ottoman Army's XV Corps under the command of Kâzım Karabekir, attacked Western Armenia with orders from the Ankara Government to "eliminate Armenia physically and politically".

slides.title: Why This Moment Matters
slides.body:
Turkish–Armenian War was more than an isolated engagement. It reflected the changing balance of power and pushed the conflict closer to its eventual outcome. The war determined whether Anatolia would be partitioned and whether a sovereign Turkish national state would replace the Ottoman order.

Consequences: The effects of Turkish–Armenian War extended beyond its immediate result. Conventional war, forced migration, communal violence, and population exchange transformed Anatolia and neighboring regions. Its place in the wider campaign also influenced later military choices and political calculations.

title: Red Army invasion of Armenia
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Red Army invasion of Armenia
slides.body: The Soviet invasion of Armenia was a military campaign which was carried out by the 11th Army of Soviet Russia from 29 November to 4 December 1920 in order to install a new Soviet government in the First Republic of Armenia, a former territory of the Russian Empire. The invasion coincided with an invasion by Kemalist Turkey and anti-government insurrections organized by local Armenian Bolsheviks. The invasion led to the dissolution of the First Republic of Armenia and the establishment of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic. Militant resistance continued in southern Armenia under Nzhdeh's self-declared Republic of Mountainous Armenia until July 1921.

title: Bombardment of Samsun
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Bombardment of Samsun
slides.body:
On 7 June 1922, ships of the Greek Navy bombarded the Turkish town of Samsun for three hours (15:02–18:00), firing 400 rounds; while in response, the single Turkish artillery piece in the town fired back 25 rounds. While the American destroyers USS Sands, USS McFarland, and USS Sturtevant were present, they did not participate in the bombardment.

Why This Moment Matters: Bombardment of Samsun was more than an isolated engagement. It reflected the changing balance of power and pushed the conflict closer to its eventual outcome. title: Chanak crisis
sub: Part of Turkish War of Independence

slides.title: Chanak crisis
slides.body: The Chanak crisis, also called the Chanak affair and the Chanak incident, was a war scare in September 1922 between the United Kingdom and the Government of the Grand National Assembly in Turkey. Chanak refers to Çanakkale, a city on the Anatolian side of the Dardanelles Strait. The crisis was caused by Turkish efforts to push the Greek armies out of Turkey and restore Turkish rule in the Allied-occupied territories, primarily in Constantinople and Eastern Thrace. Turkish troops marched against British and French positions in the Dardanelles neutral zone. For a time, war between Britain and Turkey seemed possible, but Canada refused to agree as did France and Italy. British public opinion did not want a war. The British military did not either, and the top general on the scene, Sir Charles Harington, refused to relay an ultimatum to the Turks because he counted on a negotiated settlement. The Conservatives in Britain's coalition government refused to follow Liberal Prime Minister David Lloyd George, who with Winston Churchill was calling for war.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: How the Turkish War of Independence ended and what followed

slides.title: The End of the Turkish War of Independence
slides.body: Nationalist victories overturned the proposed partition. The Treaty of Lausanne recognized the Republic of Turkey.
